title: Gunmen kill at least 10 villagers and loot shops in north-east Nigeria
description: Unknown gunmen have raided a remote village in the north-eastern Nigerian state of Taraba, killing at least 10 people, looting shops and setting house
body: Unknown gunmen have raided a remote village in the north-eastern Nigerian state of Taraba, killing at least 10 people, looting shops and setting houses ablaze, police say. There are fears the actual death toll is much higher, with eyewitnesses speaking of 20 lives lost and a non-governmental organisation suggesting a toll of as many as 50.The gunmen reportedly swooped on the village of Binnari in the Karim Lamido area mounted on motorcycles just after midday Muslim prayers on Friday in a rampage that went on for up to four hours.Police say they are searching for other casualties in the bush but the authorities were accused by Amnesty International of failing to protect rural communities.Nigeria continues to face attacks by armed groups across several regions, including the northwest, northeast and central regions.The country is also battling a jihadist insurgency in its north-east that has lasted nearly two decades, drawing persistent criticism of the government's handling of insecurity.Following the latest incident, police said they recovered 10 bodies with gunshot wounds after officers responded to a distress call.The attackers had fled by the time they arrived but they continued to patrol the area to restore calm, they told BBC News on Saturday."We were able to disperse the unknown gunmen though there was no casualty on their side and ours because the terrain is difficult and they're used to the terrain," Assistant Superintendent of Police Victor Mshelizah said.He added that officers were continuing to search the bush nearby for people who might have been killed or wounded, and warned the death toll could still rise.Community leader Malam Abubakar Saifullahi told news agency AFP that the attackers had arrived on about 50 motorcycles, two men apiece."They looted shops and took cash, foodstuffs and other provisions," he said. "They also took motorcycles abandoned by people fleeing the attack."

schema.headline: Gunmen kill at least 10 villagers and loot shops in north-east Nigeria

title: Australian MP Helen Haines' condition improves after alleged car attack
description: Nugent, who was arrested moments after he allegedly drove his Toyota LandCruiser into the MP, appeared in court to face three charges: dangerous drivi
body: Nugent, who was arrested moments after he allegedly drove his Toyota LandCruiser into the MP, appeared in court to face three charges: dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury, and causing harm to a Commonwealth public official. Police said more charges might be laid, including attempted murder.His lawyer said his client had "mental health concerns" but did not give any further detail.Victoria Police has said its investigation, with support from the Australian Federal Police, remains ongoing and a motive is yet to be established.Investigators are looking into whether drug use or medication played a part in the incident.Nugent's family has said they were long-time friends with Haines. Shortly after the alleged attack, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese told ABC television that there had been a "rise in temperature" and "too much shouting, not enough discourse" in Australia.Haines, known for stances such as supporting stronger climate action, entered parliament in 2019 after working as a nurse and midwife.

schema.headline: Australian MP Helen Haines' condition improves after alleged car attack

title: Trump administration sues to block certification of Alaska election
description: The Trump administration wants to block the certification of the Senate election in Alaska if Republican Senator Dan Sullivan loses, arguing that anot
body: The Trump administration wants to block the certification of the Senate election in Alaska if Republican Senator Dan Sullivan loses, arguing that another candidate with the same name may confuse voters.The justice department said in a federal lawsuit filed on Thursday that the inclusion of another Dan Sullivan on the ballot could lead some to mistakenly cast their votes for the wrong candidate.Polls suggest the race between Senator Sullivan and Democrat Mary Peltola is tight, with Peltola holding a narrow lead in the final days before the 3 November vote.The US government wants the judge to bar the state from certifying the results if Senator Sullivan loses by a margin less than the other Sullivan."I'm the one that said do it," US President Donald Trump told reporters when asked for his thoughts on the lawsuit after he landed in Florida for a campaign rally on Friday.Trump has referred to the second Sullivan's candidacy as a "scam" and said his administration was looking at "powerful legal options" to end it. The retired teacher previously denied his candidacy had an ulterior motive.Previous efforts to remove that Sullivan, a retired teacher, from the ballot have already been rejected by the Alaska Supreme Court.For the 3 November midterm election, the senator will be listed on the ballot as the Republican incumbent.Alaska's ranked-choice voting system means that voters could select both Sullivans if they are unsure at the ballot box.In court documents, the justice department said Alaska "will fail in its obligation to protect the integrity of its elections" if it includes "any electoral results tainted by the inclusion on the ballot of Daniel J Sullivan". The second Sullivan, who was also a US Forest Service worker, was reportedly once a member of the Alaska Independence Party before registering as a Republican earlier this year. In the filing, Associate Attorney General Stanley E Woodward Jr asserted that the sole purpose of his candidacy was to benefit Peltola's campaign by reducing the number of votes for the senator. "Given the substantial likelihood that the inclusion of Dan J Sullivan will confuse or mislead voters looking to cast a vote for Senator Sullivan and thus distort the will of Alaskan voters, there is a substantial likelihood that a certification of the election will reflect an electoral process that lacked integrity," Woodward argued.Dan J Sullivan has repeatedly denied those claims, telling the local Petersburg Pilot newspaper earlier this year that he "wouldn't even know who to speak to" in Peltola's campaign. He said separately to Courthouse News that it was his "sincere hope that people know who and what they are voting for but, ultimately, choice is good and voters' intent will be as varied as the candidates who are running".In the event Peltola wins, and the margin of loss suggests possible confusion, the lawsuit calls for certification to be delayed pending an investigation into whether voters were mixed up on the names as well as any "necessary and appropriate" steps to determine what would have happened had the second Sullivan been kept off the ballot. Neither candidate has so far commented on the lawsuit. The Senate race in Alaska - which Trump won by 14 percentage points in 2024 - is among the most closely watched in the upcoming midterm elections. The president's approval ratings in the state have been badly hit by voter disapproval of rising prices and the war in Iran.

schema.headline: Trump administration sues to block certification of Alaska election

title: Argentina drops investigation into Milei over crypto fraud
description: A criminal investigation into Argentine President Javier Milei and his sister's links to a cryptocurrency scandal has been dropped. The case against M
body: A criminal investigation into Argentine President Javier Milei and his sister's links to a cryptocurrency scandal has been dropped. The case against Milei and his sister Karina Milei was dismissed by federal judge Marcelo Martinez de Giorgi at the request of prosecutors, court records show.The Argentinian president had denied promoting the newly launched cryptocoin $Libra, which collapsed shortly after he mentioned it in a social media post in February 2025.He said he had acted "in good faith" when the cryptocurrency rose in value, before crashing and causing huge losses for the majority of its investors. Milei is yet to respond to news of the case being dropped.Dismissing the case, the judge said "the reported events do not fall under a legal category" and concluded that no "criminally relevant deception" had been proven.Accusations of fraud arose when Milei posted on X, formerly Twitter, about the $Libra coin, which he said at the time would help fund small businesses and start-ups.The cryptocurrency's price subsequently shot up when the Argentine president shared a link to buy it.But, within a few hours, he deleted his post and the crypto nosedived in value, losing investors most of their money.It led opposition members of Congress to plan impeachment proceedings, while some online accused Milei of a "rug pull" - in which promoters of a cryptocurrency draw in buyers only to stop trading activity and make off with the money raised from sales.The Argentinian president, though, insisted in an interview with Todo Noticias: "I didn't promote it, I merely shared it."The presidential office insisted that Milei was in no way involved in the development of $Libra and announced that the Anti-Corruption Office would determine whether the president had acted improperly.Milei himself defended deleting his post, saying that at the time he did not know "the details of the project and after learning about it, I decided not to continue promoting it".He insisted in a TV interview that those who had invested in $Libra had done so "voluntarily" and knew of the risks.

schema.headline: Argentina drops investigation into Milei over crypto fraud

title: Vanessa Trump says she is cancer-free six months after diagnosis
description: Vanessa Trump, the former wife of Donald Trump Jr, has announced that she is cancer-free following her breast cancer diagnosis earlier this year.Trump
body: Vanessa Trump, the former wife of Donald Trump Jr, has announced that she is cancer-free following her breast cancer diagnosis earlier this year.Trump, 48, who has five children with US President Donald Trump's eldest son, said that her recent tests results "came back clear, so I'm finally cancer-free", in a short video on her 19-year-old daughter Kai's Instagram account.Vanessa and Kai Trump then released a longer video on Saturday, in which they discussed breast cancer awareness, early detection and prevention. Vanessa Trump separated from Trump Jr in 2018 and announced last year that she had begun dating US pro golfer Tiger Woods."October is Breast Cancer Awareness Month, a time to raise awareness about early detection, education, and support for those affected by breast cancer," Kai Trump wrote on Instagram. "I sat down with my mum and Dr Nicole Saphier to talk about my mum's journey with breast cancer and learn more about prevention and early detection."Kai's post received over 20,000 likes and hundreds of comments from people offering support and well wishes, including from US singer and media personality Mary Millben. Vanessa Trump explained in the YouTube video that she experienced arm pain for several months before discovering a pea-sized lump in her breast, which testing confirmed was a cancerous tumour. "It's a process you have to deal with," she said of the days spent waiting for her test results. "You have to be mentally strong for yourself because you're going to need the strength to fight whatever challenge it is that's coming towards you."Trump said she was first diagnosed with breast cancer in April. She publicly announced the diagnosis in May, saying in a social media post that she had undergone surgery and was working on a treatment plan with her medical team. She eventually had a lumpectomy and radiation treatments, she said.The average risk of a woman in the US developing breast cancer is about 1 in 8, or 13%, according to the American Cancer Society. The disease also accounts for 30% of all new female cancers every year, it says.Surgery cures most breast cancers, but if some cancer cells remain, chemotherapy, radiotherapy and endocrine therapy can reduce the long-term risk.Treatments have been advancing, including more targeted therapies for early breast cancer, new types of hormonal therapies, and more precise and effective radiotherapy.

schema.headline: Vanessa Trump says she is cancer-free six months after diagnosis

title: Two rescued after Nairobi building collapse with five still missing
description: Two people have been pulled alive from the rubble of a building that collapsed in Kenya's capital, Nairobi, as a search continues for five still missi
body: Two people have been pulled alive from the rubble of a building that collapsed in Kenya's capital, Nairobi, as a search continues for five still missing.Dramatic footage shows the bottom floor of the block, thought to have been 16 or 18 storeys, giving way before the rest of the building crumples, sending a plume of dust into the surrounding streets on Friday. Dozens of builders had been working on the upper floors when it collapsed, but managed to emerge largely unscathed. Those missing were thought to have been in shops at the base of the building.The incident has raised fresh concerns about construction standards and regulations in Kenya.Police said on Saturday that a manhunt had been launched for the building's owner and the contractor responsible for the site.The block was under construction when it collapsed on Friday afternoon, with footage showing scaffolding still wrapped around the outside of the building. Officials said 11 shops had already opened on the bottom floors.Interior ministry official Kipchumba Murkomen said 66 of the 67 construction workers in the building at the time had been able to get out unharmed, while the other had suffered injuries that were not life-threatening.He had said on Friday that seven people had been reported missing and rescue teams had made contact with some of those trapped beneath the rubble.The two survivors rescued on Saturday have been taken to hospital, police said.Images from the scene, in Nairobi's Eastleigh area, show the concrete floors of the building piled on top of one another, as rescue workers saw through metal to get to those believed to have been stuck underneath.

schema.headline: Two rescued after Nairobi building collapse with five still missing

title: Brazil election: Voters to choose between Lula and Bolsonaro's son
description: Never before has a candidate who trailed after the first round managed to overturn the deficit and win in the second round.Bolsonaro's supporters were
body: Never before has a candidate who trailed after the first round managed to overturn the deficit and win in the second round.Bolsonaro's supporters were jubilant at his final campaign rallies, confident that he would bring change to Brazil through his promised tough crackdown on organised crime, as well as tax and public spending cuts. He campaigned on the eve of polls in Belo Horizonte, the capital of Minas Gerais, which has been a must-win state for any presidential hopeful since the 1980s."The time is almost here," Bolsonaro told supporters in a social media video."There are only a few hours left before we shape the future of our nation for the next 30 or 40 years." He has also pledged to release his father, who is currently serving his sentence under house arrest due to ill health. In Barra de Tijuca, Rio de Janeiro, where Jair Bolsonaro has a home, Bolsonaro supporters rallied in support of him dressed in the national colours."Brazil needs change, and Flávio is the person that represents that today, after so many years of the Left destroying the economy and the country," one told BBC News.Another said that what she most liked about Flávio Bolsonaro was his promise to "end violence in Brazil, end terrorism, narco-trafficking, and to reduce interest rates".

schema.headline: Brazil election: Voters to choose between Lula and Bolsonaro's son

title: Musk says SpaceX restricted Ukraine's Starlink connection as service restored
description: Elon Musk has said his company SpaceX restricted Ukraine's Starlink internet service, after Ukrainian officials said connectivity issues appeared to h
body: Elon Musk has said his company SpaceX restricted Ukraine's Starlink internet service, after Ukrainian officials said connectivity issues appeared to have been resolved.The tech billionaire accused Ukraine of violating its terms of service by using it for military activity - but denied being responsible for a simultaneous issue with its US-run, military-grade counterpart Starshield.Kyiv has not officially commented on Musk's latest claim but Ukrainian presidential adviser Serhiy Beskrestnov said his post was "very strange".Musk had earlier denied deliberately throttling Ukraine's connection, which it says hampered its ability to conduct defensive operations.The issue first emerged last week during a broader row between Washington and Kyiv over Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil infrastructure.Musk's latest comments, and the seeming restoration of the service, came after US President Donald Trump said he had told the Tesla and X owner to "put it back", having repeatedly denied instructing him to limit the service."Using Starlink, a civilian commercial service, for offensive drone strikes to kill people has never been allowed, nor should it be," Musk wrote on X on Saturday. "Ukraine['s] military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week."He went on to say that SpaceX had "done more to defend Ukraine than any private company on Earth" and reiterated his stipulation that Starshield was a different system and controlled by the US government, adding: "What they decide to do is up to them."He added in a later post: "[Starlink] can be used for infrastructure that is military, but it cannot be used for unequivocally offensive strikes that make it fair game to be struck back."Reacting to Musk's post, Beskrestnov wrote on Telegram that Ukraine "physically cannot use" commercial Starlink for long- and middle-range drone strikes.There was no immediate comment from the country's defence ministry.Ukraine uses both the civilian service Starlink and the more secure Starshield, depending on what communications are needed, both of which run on networks of low Earth orbit satellites launched by SpaceX.Starlink allows military units to co-ordinate, particularly in remote areas on the battlefield, while Starshield allows Ukrainian drone operators to see targets in real time, as well as operate interceptor drones.Russia is not authorised to use Starlink, so when Ukraine sends long-range missiles or drones deep into Russia to hit oil refineries, the network does not work.Ukraine's Defence Minister Yevhenii Khmara said earlier on Saturday that the military was now recording a "stable connection", with drones now able to reach speeds in excess of 400km/h (249mph). Kyiv previously said the connection would cut out above 161km/h."The speeds are now where they need to be," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky wrote on Telegram. Musk did not disclose in his post why SpaceX had chosen to make the change to its service last week, when Ukraine's extensive use of Starlink had been known for several years.The connection issues coincided with a tense diplomatic standoff between Zelensky and Trump over Ukrainian strikes on oil infrastructure within Russia.Trump said the strikes on Russian oil refineries, which Kyiv says are crucial to stemming the main revenue source for Moscow's war effort, have pushed global prices higher.While the attacks have had an impact on global fuel prices, rises seen this year have primarily been due to the Iran war.Faced with midterm elections next month and domestic displeasure with rising fuel prices, Trump waived some sanctions on Russia and agreed a deal with Moscow - criticised by European allies as funding Russia's war machine - to supply Russian diesel to the US and the global market.Zelensky initially agreed to do so on the proviso that Russia cease striking Ukraine's energy infrastructure, before restarting the strikes after several instances of Moscow disregarding this.The Ukrainian leader said that, as well as seemingly limiting Starlink capability in Ukraine, the US had also threatened to withdraw intelligence sharing if the strikes did not stop, something Trump also denied.

schema.headline: Musk says SpaceX restricted Ukraine's Starlink connection as service restored

title: Minneapolis withdrawal was 'surrender', Trump's ex-border patrol chief says
description: The former US border patrol chief who became the public face of the highly controversial deportation drive in Minneapolis earlier this year has defend
body: The former US border patrol chief who became the public face of the highly controversial deportation drive in Minneapolis earlier this year has defended the operation, describing the withdrawal of agents from the city as a "surrender" by the Trump administration.Greg Bovino also told the BBC that he was "not responding" to a lawsuit filed by the family of a woman shot dead during the operation. He appeared to dismiss the legal action, praising the officers deployed to Minneapolis and saying "people do lawsuits all the time".Bovino, 56, was removed from his role shortly after the fatal shootings of US citizens Renee Good and Alex Pretti in January.The two shootings, which were captured on video, triggered a bipartisan backlash and widespread protests. US President Donald Trump then said he was "going to de-escalate a little bit" and withdrew hundreds of immigration agents from the city.Earlier this month, Good's family filed two civil lawsuits against the Trump administration over her killing, alleging wrongful death and a conspiracy to interfere with the civil rights of protesters.One of the lawsuits names several top officials, including Bovino and Jonathan Ross, the agent who shot Good, "for their respective individual roles in the operation that led to Renee's death". It alleges that the government's operation in Minneapolis created "an unprecedented environment for state-sponsored violence".Asked about Bovino's remarks, the family's lawyers said he was "spewing propaganda" and could not be "judge, jury and executioner". They added: "Our legal team looks forward to the depositions of Mr Bovino and all of the defendants in this matter".A White House spokeswoman previously called the lawsuits "baseless".Speaking in Detroit, where he was campaigning for tougher immigration enforcement, Bovino said the administration "threw the towel in" and called for more deportations, which he said were now at a "virtual standstill".He added that he regretted "not going harder in Minnesota and arresting even more illegal aliens".Bovino said his agents in Minneapolis were the "real victims" of what he called "the most violence that any law enforcement mission ever in the history of the United States has been up against".Challenged by the BBC over how immigration agents handled both shooting incidents, Bovino rejected suggestions that video evidence undermined his claim that Good and Pretti had intended to harm the agents."The evidence is that violence was perpetrated against agents of the US government, and this is a society of laws and people need to follow the law. If not, there are consequences," he said.Trump initially blamed Good's own actions for her death, saying just hours after she was killed that she "violently, willfully and viciously ran over the ICE officer". Weeks later, he called her death a "tragedy" and said agents were sometimes "going to make a mistake".The withdrawal from Minnesota, which saw some 700 immigration agents leave the state, also saw Bovino removed from his post. The operation was taken over by the White House 'border tsar' Tom Homan.When asked why he was removed, Bovino told the BBC: "You'd have to ask the administration. I still haven't gotten the final word on that."

schema.headline: Minneapolis withdrawal was 'surrender', Trump's ex-border patrol chief says

title: Macron says deadly shooting near Paris is a 'racist terrorist attack'
description: French President Emmanuel Macron has labelled a gun attack in a Parisian suburb that killed one person and injured five others "a racist terrorist att
body: French President Emmanuel Macron has labelled a gun attack in a Parisian suburb that killed one person and injured five others "a racist terrorist attack".Macron said the attack was a "turning point in the life of our Republic and our nation" - the first time there had ever been a random racial killing like this.The attack unfolded over some 15 minutes, with the attacker opening fire from his car - first in Trappes, to the south-west of Paris, and then in nearby La Verrière - appearing to target people of migrant origin. He was subsequently arrested.Three of those injured, including a 12-year-old girl, remain in a serious condition.Macron said while visiting the scene of the attack that people had been targeted over their skin colour or religion and urged the public not to give an inch in the face of what he called "ideologies taking root".The exact motive remains unclear, but the National Anti-Terrorist Prosecutor's Office (PNAT) said the incident appeared to be "murder in connection with a terrorist enterprise".The suspect has been named in French media as Kevin T who, according to PNAT, had four previous convictions that had been "automatically expunged".The 39-year-old was known to police but not to France's intelligence services, local media report.He was not on a list of individuals considered to be a serious threat to French security, the national anti-terrorism prosecutor's office told BFMTV.A member of the suspect's "immediate family circle" was also taken into custody on Friday, it added.

schema.headline: Macron says deadly shooting near Paris is a 'racist terrorist attack'

title: Israel to close West Bank crossings on election day as crackdown escalates
description: All West Bank land crossings will be closed during Tuesday's election in Israel, the country's military says, and Palestinian workers will be barred f
body: All West Bank land crossings will be closed during Tuesday's election in Israel, the country's military says, and Palestinian workers will be barred from entering all settlements.The restrictions come amid a crackdown in the occupied West Bank after Palestinian gunmen killed two Israeli soldiers in the territory.The Israel Defense Forces announced a "ban on the entry and exit of Palestinian workers throughout Judea and Samaria and the Jordan Valley, including industrial zones, as well as the closure of all land crossings" on Tuesday.It said most workers would also be barred from settlements from Sunday, with the exception of industrial zones and a limited number of other areas.Before the Hamas-led October 7, 2023 attack on Israel, more than 100,000 Palestinian workers were permitted to enter Israel. Since then only a small fraction have had their permits restored.Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu announced a major operation on Friday in response to the killing of two Israeli soldiers by two Palestinian gunmen in an attack on a checkpoint. Three other Israeli soldiers were injured, and the gunmen were also killed.The Israeli military have been demolishing homes and businesses in the city of Hebron, with hundreds of families having been displaced. Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz said about 2,000 residents had been displaced by the operation, which has led to at least one whole street appearing to have been flattened, according to footage shared online.Even before the entry and exit bans on workers were announced by the IDF on Sunday, the military had cordoned off the city, heavily restricting the movement of its 200,000 residents.It is common for Israeli forces to demolish the homes of Palestinians who are suspected of carrying out attacks on Israelis in the West Bank - a practice Israeli rights groups have criticised as collective punishment.Friday's shooting came during a tense time for the region, just days ahead of Israel's election taking place on Tuesday.In an interview with Israel's i24 television channel released on Saturday, Netanyahu threatened a "very big surprise" for the Palestinian Authority (PA), which governs parts of the territory.Hebron Mayor Youssef al-Jaabari said the operation was being "driven by the elections" and that Netanyahu and his ministers were attempting to secure the votes of the far right and the settlers.On Saturday, thousands gathered in Tel Aviv for a large anti-government demonstration.The protest was organised by the October Council, a group founded by the families of victims and hostages taken by militants on 7 October 2023, to demand accountability for the failure to prevent the Hamas-led attack."Three days before the election, we will hold the culminating event marking three years of struggle to uncover the truth, demand accountability, and establish a state commission of inquiry," the October Council wrote on X ahead of the rally.The gathering saw the participation of the leaders of the four main opposition parties, including Gadi Eisenkot, the former military chief of staff who is neck and neck with Netanyahu.

schema.headline: Israel to close West Bank crossings on election day as crackdown escalates

title: Obama attacks Trump as he campaigns for Democrats ahead of midterm elections
description: Former US President Barack Obama has attacked the Trump administration over the Iran war and high consumer prices as he hit the campaign trail for Dem
body: Former US President Barack Obama has attacked the Trump administration over the Iran war and high consumer prices as he hit the campaign trail for Democrats ahead of the US midterm elections."This election is our last best chance to at least rein in some of the foolishness of this administration," Obama told crowds in Ohio on Saturday.Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump touted his administration's immigration and tariff policies at a rally in Georgia, telling supporters "we're in the golden age of America". The midterm elections on 3 November will decide which party controls Congress for the rest of Trump's term, and therefore how easy it is for the president to carry out his plans.Early voting has already begun and Trump cast his ballot on Saturday in Florida alongside his wife First Lady Melania Trump.Obama targeted Trump and his cabinet members while speaking on Saturday in Ohio and Michigan, at one point mocking the president's attempt to redecorate the White House."After two years of chaos and cruelty and corruption and incompetence, the likes of which we have not seen in the modern era, you get a chance to say, 'enough is enough'," the former president said in Cleveland. Obama said he sympathised with voters who rejected Democrats in 2024 over economic and inflation concerns following the Covid pandemic. But he said Trump had only himself to blame for the current state of the economy. "If you thought everything was too expensive before 'you know who'," he said, referring to Trump without using his name, "everything is more expensive now".Trump, meanwhile, acknowledged that oil prices were "temporarily high" but said "our country is getting stronger and stronger all the time, and those pump prices are going to come down".The Republican president has faced significant pressure to lower fuel prices, which have jumped due to the wars in Iran and Ukraine.Talking up the economy, Trump told the crowd in Perry "we're taking in massive amounts of money through tariffs" and repeated his pledge to offer every adult American a $5,000 (£3,700) payout if Republicans win both chambers of Congress.He also took aim at the Democrats, telling the crowd they would "loot your wealth" and "annihilate your borders".Using derogatory language, he accused the Democrats of trying to open up immigration from Libya, Yemen, Haiti and Somalia - countries which he described as "terror-infested".Describing a previous meeting with several senators, he recalled: "I said, 'Why do we always have to take people from shithouse countries? Why can't we take people from, like, well... Norway, Sweden? Why not Denmark?'"

schema.headline: Obama attacks Trump as he campaigns for Democrats ahead of midterm elections

title: Husband's tribute to British woman who died after rescuing son in the Bahamas
description: Mum who died trying to save sons was hero, husband saysImage source, SuppliedImage caption, The Royal Bahamas Police Force said officers on the island
body: Mum who died trying to save sons was hero, husband saysImage source, SuppliedImage caption, The Royal Bahamas Police Force said officers on the island of Bimini launched an investigation into the sudden death of Leanne Gregory on TuesdayByBen CarrEast MidlandsThe husband of a British woman who died rescuing their sons when they were swept away to sea in the Bahamas says she was a "hero... in life and in death".Leanne Gregory, from Stapleford in Nottinghamshire, had been snorkelling with her family when the boys were swept away by a strong current, police said. Although the children were rescued from the water off the island of Bimini on Tuesday, their mother was unable to be saved, the Royal Bahamas Police Force said.Nathan Gregory said the loss of his 36-year-old "childhood sweetheart" was "unimaginable for our family".'Absolute hero'"She was the purest, most amazing wife, mother and friend to have ever walked this Earth," her husband said in a Facebook post."I will never get over this, she was my soulmate, my childhood sweetheart, my one and only. The foundation of my entire family and the strength that held us all together."My boys had to witness something nobody should ever have to see of any age, but they know Mum died an absolute hero."Gregory said he had also set up a fundraising page "for my sons and security after the tragic loss".In the post on that page he described how his wife, who he had been with for 22 years, had held on to their son until he was rescued "but didn't have the energy to save herself".He added: "I just have to be thankful for the hero she was in life and in death, and totally grateful for the fact my boys got out safely."Image source, NurPhoto/Getty ImagesImage caption, The two children were rescued off the coast of Bimini, police in the Bahamas saidIn a statement posted on social media, the Royal Bahamas Police Force said officers received reports shortly after 10:00 local time on Tuesday that a woman had been found unresponsive at the North Bimini Ferry Dock.It added after she was swept away, she was brought to the ferry dock where CPR was given.Mrs Gregory was then taken to a local medical clinic but was confirmed dead there, the police force said.It said an autopsy would be conducted but "foul play is not suspected".A spokesperson for the Foreign Office added: "Our thoughts are with the family of a British woman who has died in the Bahamas."We are in contact with the local authorities and providing support to her family."Get in touchTell us which stories we should cover in Nottingham

schema.headline: Husband's tribute to British woman who died after rescuing son in the Bahamas

title: Almost 1,000 arrested as clashes follow another day of mass protests across France
description: Figure caption, Watch: BBC in Paris as police charge protesters during skirmishesByJaroslav LukivUpdated 4 hours agoNearly 1,000 arrests were made as
body: Figure caption, Watch: BBC in Paris as police charge protesters during skirmishesByJaroslav LukivUpdated 4 hours agoNearly 1,000 arrests were made as hundreds of thousands of people took part in another day of protests across France, which were followed by some clashes late on Saturday, officials have said.After a day of largely peaceful demonstrations, police fired tear gas and water cannon to disperse protesters in a number of cities including Paris, while barricades were set alight in Marseille and people ripped boards from a shop in Bordeaux.But officials have so far managed to avoid rioting and looting on the scale seen last weekend, which resulted in some of the worst scenes of disorder in France's modern history.The interior ministry said an estimated 410,000 people protested on Saturday, while the unions put the number at about 800,000.Some 70,000 police officers were deployed and restrictions imposed in several cities to prevent the latest protests over the cost of living and poor school conditions from descending into the kind of chaos which saw officers outnumbered, hundreds of businesses looted and buildings torched.President Emmanuel Macron had decreed earlier this week that only demonstrations organised by a recognised trade unions would be permitted. Hundreds of people have been jailed for vandalism, arson and looting after fast-track court hearings in recent days.Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, In the southern port of Marseille, protesters erected makeshift street barricades and set them alight late on SaturdayClashes between protesters and riot police in Paris erupted at the end of a peaceful march from the city's Porte d'Italie towards Porte de Vincennes on Saturday, where the police operation included an elite unit that usually deals with organised crime and counter-terrorism.Some protesters were seen erecting makeshift barricades and pelting officers with projectiles, while police baton-charged groups of masked youths who were smashing the windows of a car dealership.French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said that "several thousand radical activists gathered at the rear of the march, including around 500 individuals identified as rioters", the AFP news agency reported.Image source, EPAImage caption, Protesters clash with police at a demonstration in BordeauxIn the southern port of Marseille, rubbish bins were set ablaze and metal sheets used to block streets. A law enforcement vehicle was seen driving through a burning barricade in France's second-largest city.Meanwhile, some protesters in dark clothing and face coverings were seen taking boards off a building to build a street barricade in the southern city of Bordeaux.In Lyon, police used tear gas grenades to disperse a crowd which had reportedly gathered in an area deemed off-limits by the local prefecture."There were around 150 of us, mostly secondary school and university students. Then the tear gas came almost immediately. You could barely see anything in the street," said one protester in France's third-largest city.Nuñez said late in the day that nearly 1,000 people had been arrested, a number he said would increase.The minister also said two people had been "seriously injured": one in the south-western city of Toulouse, and another one in Clermont-Ferrand, central France.Image caption, "We really want a change in France," a teenage protester told the BBCEarlier, a peaceful protester in Paris who gave her name as Zelie told the BBC people had taken to the streets because they were "really frustrated" and had been "suffering a lot" since Macron came to office."They keep us quiet. They take our money, they tax us a lot and we can't say anything. Today we are in the streets because it's been too long, it's been too much," the 26-year-old said.Two masked teenage protesters, who did not want to give their names, also said their generation was in despair and felt abandoned by the government."I think looting is really not good," one of the demonstrators said of last Saturday's disorder. "But it's because of poverty and the violence of the police."He added that the protests would end "when we have a response to our demands. We really want a change in France".Image source, ReutersMeanwhile, some 13,000 people joined a rally against the hard-right National Rally party in the north-central city of Orléans which proceeded peacefully.Mass protests triggered by similar issues as in France also rocked several other European cities on Saturday.In Barcelona, more than 100 people were arrested after a student protest descended into what local authorities described as "gratuitous violence". In Albania's capital Tirana, riot police fired tear gas to disperse thousands of anti-government demonstrators, while clashes were also reported in Belgium's capital Brussels.In Milan, northern Italy, a major security operation including hundreds of soldiers alongside police prevented protesters gathering in the city. Many had feared a repeat of violent scenes last week when some started fires, smashed windows and looted shops.Image source, EPAImage caption, People clash with police during a demonstration against the high cost of living in Bordeaux.Around 550,000 people took part in last weekend's demonstrations against rising fuel prices and the cost of living, with frustrations escalating after weeks of student protests. The chaos which followed resulted in more than 2,500 arrests.Marches were initially largely peaceful but became marred by scenes of violence, looting and destruction, with more than 2,000 shops and other businesses across France said to have been directly impacted. The damage was estimated "at hundreds of millions euros", France's Chambers of Commerce and Industry (CCI) said.One demonstrator's hand was blown off by a police crowd-control grenade, according to the AFP news agency, while about 1,000 police officers were injured.The French authorities later said they were forced to impose overnight curfews in Paris and other cities.The continuing protests come ahead of France's presidential elections in six months' time, and leading contenders have levelled the blame at Macron and his ministers.

schema.headline: Almost 1,000 arrested as clashes follow another day of mass protests across France

title: White House says Melania Trump brokers truce for Ukraine city 'on brink of disaster'
description: The White House statement said Melania Trump and one of her representatives had worked "directly with Russian and Ukrainian leadership to define the t
body: The White House statement said Melania Trump and one of her representatives had worked "directly with Russian and Ukrainian leadership to define the terms of the localised ceasefire"."Non-military, civilian leaders from both countries will work together to visit Oleshky residents in their homes and determine the level of assistance they require," she is quoted as saying."Residents who wish to evacuate will receive co-ordinated support and transportation to their preferred destination. I anticipate some will want to go to Russia, and some to Ukraine."Melania Trump added that Oleshky residents "have limited electricity, live amid mined roads, and endure regular military attacks" and that "without my intervention, the possibility to bring humanitarian aid into the city and to evacuate the elderly would be impossible".The statement did not say how long the ceasefire would be in place for.Davyd Arakhamia, a Ukrainian MP who heads President Volodymyr Zelensky's party in parliament, later said "an operation to unblock the settlement of Oleshky and its surroundings will begin in the near future"."To achieve this goal, a ceasefire will be achieved in the near future, as announced by the First Lady of the United States, Melania Trump," he said.In Russia, President Vladimir Putin's spokesman confirmed that, "those who wish to do so will be able to leave this settlement".Last month, some of the remaining Oleshky residents told the BBC harrowing accounts of how they were surviving in the city that was being constantly shelled and cut off from food and water.They said that children remaining in wider Oleshky were suffering from malnutrition, a lack of medical services and were "degrading" without access to education.Many also told the BBC there was only one hospital partially operational, opening a few days a week to perform critical amputations.The local population was living under a "full blockade" by Russian forces, according to Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha.Ukraine says it has attempted to deliver supplies to the area but has not had success in recent months.The Kremlin in September acknowledged that Oleshky was facing "a critical situation" and "problems with supplies of food and medicine", but added that "Russia's military was working to resolve them" and blamed Kyiv.The Pope had been among those urging a ceasefire in the city, calling for "dialogue and peace".Oleshky was home to 24,000 people before Russia's full-scale invasion. Now  Ukraine estimates that some 6,000 people remain in the city and its surrounding areas, including 200 children.It is also one of a number of settlements where thousands of people lost their homes to a massive flooding caused by the collapse of Nova Khakovka Dam in 2023. Ukraine and its allies accused Russia of blowing up the dam, while Russia blamed Ukraine.While the US first lady is relatively lower profile than some of her predecessors - and only occasionally seen at White House events - she has become involved in addressing humanitarian issues stemming from the Russia-Ukraine war.In August 2025, Melania Trump penned a letter to Putin, telling him it was "time to protect children and future generations worldwide".Although she did not mention Ukraine by name, just days later at the White House Zelensky handed over a letter from his wife Olena, thanking her for her efforts on children.In a rare public appearance in October the same year, the US first lady said that Putin had answered directly in writing and that her representatives were working with the Russian president's team to repatriate Ukrainian children from Russia and vice versa.Some 34 children have reportedly been returned since 2025, including five this July.According to US President Donald Trump, his wife has also privately expressed scepticism about Putin and his desire to achieve peace."I'd get home, I'd say, 'First lady, I had the most wonderful talk with Vladimir. I think we're finished'," Trump said in July last year."And then I'll turn on the television, or she'll say to me one time, 'Wow, that's strange because they just bombed a nursing home.'"

schema.headline: White House says Melania Trump brokers truce for Ukraine city 'on brink of disaster'
